data.title: Government contractor arrested for allegedly leaking national defense information
data.description:
Federal authorities arrested a government contractor and charged him with leaking classified national defense information, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced on Friday.

FBI investigators have accused 42-year-old Ian Brinksman, an employee of a third-party company which provided services to a government agency, of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, who writes an online publication on Substack.

“A fundraising article reportedly published by Individual 1 in September 2026 claimed Individual 1 had “published reporting based on classified [relevant U.S. government agency] assessments.” Individual 1 posted on her social media profile, “I also accept leaks,” the DOJ said in its release.

Brinkman was arrested following a search of his Washington, D.C., home.

Quotes included in the affidavit match the description of posts to the Capital & Empire Substack, a Congress and defense publication written by Aida Chavez.

Chavez did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment. Chavez’s past work has appeared in The Hill, according to her bio on the social platform X.

In the DOJ’s statement announcing Brinkman’s arrest, FBI Director Kash Patel said any employee caught leaking classified information will “be met with the full weight of justice.”

“Protecting America’s secrets is a top counterintelligence priority of this FBI – and anyone caught abusing their position of trust within the government by jeopardizing national security and putting our brave warriors at risk will be met with the full weight of justice,” Patel said.

Identifying and prosecuting leakers has been a priority for the second Trump administration, threatening prosecution of both the government employees and media organizations that publish leaks.

In July, the DOJ moved to subpoena four journalists from The New York Times for their reporting on a luxury jet gifted to the president by Qatar, which was used as Air Force One but has periodically been pulled for security concerns.

Trump is not the first president to vow to go after leakers or to subpoena journalists — former presidents Obama, George W. Bush and Nixon did the same.

data.title: 'You have this superpower' — how the left is weaponizing jury nullification
data.description:
“You have this superpower.”

That statement from Qiana Johnson is part of reported training material for residents to engage in “jury nullification,” whereby jurors ignore the law and incriminating facts in a given case to nullify any prosecution.

Notably, Johnson is the newly elected clerk of Prince George’s County Circuit Court in the Maryland suburbs of Washington. She is part of a growing left-wing movement gaining traction with voters that calls for radical changes to the U.S. legal system.  

The effort is to engineer “Twelve Angry Men” scenarios on real juries — but unlike in the movie, the jurors are actually being trained to ignore evidence and deliberations in favor of political outcomes.

In her election campaign for her current job, Johnson had to overcome questions about her own criminal record. But many voters are willing to give others a second chance when they show evidence of rehabilitation and contrition. The more immediate concern might be embracing a practice that is expressly barred by courts.

Johnson is part of a new investigation by the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee into groups training citizens to engage in jury nullification — including Free DC and Harriet’s Wildest Dreams, where Johnson was reportedly a board member.

One such document allegedly declares, “You have this superpower, and that superpower is you are able to nullify that goddamn jury.”

Far-left professors have long advocated that juries use jury nullification. Georgetown Law professor and MSNBC legal analyst Paul Butler has long advocated that Black jurors engage in nullification in cases involving Black defendants. Butler wrote in the Washington Post in 2016: “Confronting the racial crisis in criminal justice, jury nullification gives jurors a special power to send the message that Black lives matter.”

The problem of biased jurors has long plagued the legal system. It can work both ways in ignoring the law to refuse or secure convictions. Past cases involving President Trump and other Republicans have raised bias concerns over the jury pool in cities such as Washington, D.C., and New York City.  

But jury nullification is different; it is a direct assault on the very foundation of the American court system. The juror is the thumping heart of that system — a group of empowered citizens who swear to consider cases without prejudice or prejudgment.

It is not a crime to advocate jury nullification. Moreover, there are legitimate concerns raised by investigations into such groups. about chilling the rights of free speech and association. In my view, such advocacy is protected speech under the First Amendment. 

But that is not always the case for lawyers, who can face professional consequences. Many courts bar lawyers from arguing for jury nullification. Calling for jury nullification can also present sanctionable conduct for lawyers in a given case.

Even if this is protected speech, voices in both parties need to denounce these efforts. It effectively encourages jurors to lie when they take their oath to follow the law and to shed any outside bias or prejudgment. It is an effort to enlist jurors in using cases to achieve political and social goals at the expense of the rule of law.

The professors and pundits supporting these campaigns are actively seeking a hostile takeover of the courts without explaining to these citizens the implications of such dishonesty. Indeed, Comer has detailed how groups like Freedom Trainers are allegedly seeking to enlist potential jurors while, according to the committee, instructing trainees not to “signal the agenda.”

Instead of addressing the impact of politicizing our jurors, these groups are portraying nullification as “a powerful tool for ensuring fairness and justice.”

These efforts are coming at a time of full assault on our judicial system from the left. Leading Democrats are calling for the packing of the Supreme Court, to reverse decisions with which they disagree. Every leading Democratic candidate for the 2028 presidential nomination has now thrown the court to the baying mob.

Former Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton is only the most recent, declaring, “We should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.”

From the trial jury to the Supreme Court, many on the left now seek to take control of institutions that have long been the rock of this Republic. If successful, justice will become merely an extension of politics.

What is so disconcerting is that there is no longer any pretense of principle. Law professors are demanding that pledges to pack the Court be used as litmus tests for politicians, and senators are calling for an instant liberal majority on the Court to carry out the “will of the people.” 

Liberal professors have long demanded revolutionary change to “reclaim America from constitutionalism.”

The attack on the American jury may be the most insidious of these efforts. Our legal system invests average citizens with the power to do justice. Every community plays a role in upholding the principles of blind justice. As with court-packing, jury nullification is a previously odious practice now being portrayed as a noble cause. It is part of the conditioning of voters to accept foundational changes to our constitutional system, to further a radical agenda harmful to the nation.

The juror’s role was indeed a “superpower,” but not the one these professors and pundits are pushing. It was a power against prejudice and partisanship; it was the power of doing simple justice in a nation committed to the rule of law.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.”

data.title: Trump hints that White House press area may be moved to another location
data.description:
President Trump pushed back Saturday morning against reports he was considering replacing the White House press briefing room with an indoor swimming pool but said he was considering moving media “to a less obnoxious location.”

On Tuesday, The New York Times reported Trump expressed to aides he would like to bring back an indoor pool installed in 1933 during the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration. The pool was later covered under former President Richard Nixon to make space for the briefing room. 

“There is a Fake News report out there that I am going to remove the White House Press Room and bring back the old Swimming Pool, which lies directly underneath,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. 

“Although I may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location, the old swimming pool will never be brought back,” he continued. “I NEVER even thought to do such a stupid thing!”

The president and his administration have increasingly sought to restrict press access due to unfavorable reporting throughout his second term.

This week, the White House stripped The Independent’s Andrew Feinberg of his print press pool duties, barring him from traveling with the president after Trump lashed out at the reporter in the Oval Office. 

White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) President Jacqui Heinrich accused the White House of acting in “retaliation.”

“The American public’s right to an independent press depends on reporters being able to do their jobs without fear that challenging the president will cut off their access,” Heinrich said in a statement. 

A White House spokesperson defended the move in a Wednesday evening statement to The Hill. 

“No person and no journalist has a constitutional right to access the President’s Oval Office, Air Force One, or other sensitive and private facilities,” the spokesperson said. “When publications lie, fabricate, and ignore the truth, proximity matters less and they can write their fiction from outside of these secure facilities.” 

Last month, the WHCA also condemned the Trump administration’s decision to bar Politico, CNN and MS NOW from the White House. The move drew widespread criticism and an order from a federal judge to reinstate the media credentials to journalists from these outlets. Though CNN reporters, like Feinberg, are still unable to join the press pool on Air Force One.

data.title: DOJ demands California counties identify noncitizen voters: Reports
data.description:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday sent letters to election officials in every California county asking that they identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls, according to several reports. 

The letter warned local officials would “risk significant federal scrutiny” if they failed to comply with this request, The New York Times reported, citing a spokesperson for the U.S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles. 

The DOJ’s letters included a list of people federal officials claimed the agency has identified as possible noncitizens who may receive ballots through California’s practice of sending a ballot to every registered voter in the state. 

The DOJ gave local officials 48 hours “to identify who on the accompanying list is a citizen and who is not.” 

For those whose “citizenship status cannot be confirmed, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate — not cancel — those individuals vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined,” the letter said, according to the Times. 

The top federal prosecutor in Southern California, Bill Essayli, said in a statement shared on social media that the request was “simple.”

“California does not verify citizenship status. We did the work for them,” he wrote. “We obtained the registered voter list and told them who we believe are noncitizens on their rolls. 

“Knowingly processing noncitizen ballots is a federal crime under 18 U.S.C. §§ 611 and 2,” he continued. “We will hold election officials accountable. No one is above the law.”

The demand comes 11 days before the midterm elections, and it follows the Trump administration’s repeated warnings that significant numbers of noncitizens are registered to vote in this election. 

The Trump administration sued California last week after the DOJ threatened legal action if state and local election officials refused to cross-reference 20,000 names on its voter rolls with information provided by the Department of Homeland Security. 

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) accused President Trump of “trying to quite literally rig the election” in his state during a campaign event in New Hampshire on Sunday. 

“He’s trying to get our voting rolls,” he said. “You can’t make this stuff up.”

data.title: A dangerous El Niño could turn hunger into famine
data.description:
Much of the world’s attention today is fixed on election campaigns, polls, predictions and political battles. Headlines are dominated by who is up, who is down and what comes next. 

But while candidates compete for votes, another race is unfolding far from the campaign trail: a race against hunger that millions of families are in danger of losing. 

Today, more than 266 million people face acute food insecurity. Yet hunger rarely becomes a headline until it reaches catastrophic levels. By the time images of starving children appear on our screens, families have often been suffering for months, even years. 

Famine doesn’t arrive all at once. It arrives slowly, harvest by harvest, meal by meal, until suddenly the world is asking how things got so bad. 

The warning signs are already here. Now, a new threat is gathering strength.

Recent forecasts warn that the developing 2026-27 El Niño weather phenomenon could bring drought, flooding, crop losses and rising food insecurity across some of the world’s most vulnerable regions. East and Southern Africa are among the areas of particular concern, where additional climate shocks could drive sharply higher humanitarian needs. 

Frontline international humanitarian organizations are reaching a similar conclusion: the developing El Niño could push millions more people into hunger, with particularly severe consequences for women and girls, children and communities already affected by conflict and displacement. Their analyses point to growing food and nutrition risks and worsening food insecurity in places such as Somalia. 

Parents are skipping meals so their children can eat. Families are selling livestock and other assets to survive. Children are leaving school, while communities that have already endured conflict, displacement and economic hardship are being pushed closer to the edge. 

Now, a new threat is gathering strength. 

Recent forecasts warn that the developing 2026-27 El Niño could bring drought, flooding, crop losses and rising food insecurity across some of the world’s most vulnerable regions. East and Southern Africa are among the areas of particular concern, where additional climate shocks could drive sharply higher humanitarian needs. 

The danger is not drought alone. It is the collision of multiple crises. 

Conflict continues to disrupt food production and trade. Economic pressures are driving up the costs of food, fertilizer and transportation. At the same time, humanitarian resources are shrinking just as needs are increasing. For millions of families already struggling to recover from previous shocks, there is little margin left. 

But hunger is one of the few global crises we can often see coming. Early warning systems provide something rare in humanitarian response: a chance to act before lives are lost and communities are pushed into catastrophe. 

In fact, some early action is underway. The U.S. government recently announced additional support to help Peru prepare for El Niño-related impacts, underscoring a simple truth: acting on early warnings saves lives and reduces the far greater costs of responding after a crisis takes hold. But more is needed.

Across the globe, American humanitarian organizations are already working alongside local partners to help communities prepare for additional shocks. They are supporting farmers, strengthening local food systems, protecting livelihoods and helping vulnerable families withstand crises. These efforts rarely make headlines, but they can determine whether a shock becomes a hardship or a humanitarian disaster. 

As Congress and the administration make decisions about funding and priorities for the year ahead, they face a straightforward choice: act on the warnings we already have or wait until preventable suffering becomes a full-blown humanitarian emergency that is far more costly, both financially and humanly. 

Hunger is not inevitable. We know the warning signs. We know what works. The question is whether we choose to act before today’s warning becomes tomorrow’s crisis. 

Tom Hart is president and CEO of InterAction, the national alliance of U.S.-based nongovernmental organizations.

data.title: Live Updates: Obama, Harris to campaign for Democrats in 3 battleground states; Trump travels to Georgia
data.description:
President Trump has held rallies throughout the week in Iowa, Kansas, Florida and more, but leaders of the Democratic Party are set to hold a midterm blitz of their own on Saturday ahead of Election Day.

Former President Obama is expected to make two Midwest trips to Cleveland, Ohio and Detroit, Mich. to help move the needle for Democrats in the two battleground states.

Obama will first travel to Ohio to hold a rally with former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who is locked in a tight battle with Ohio Republican Jon Husted for the Buckeye State’s Senate seat.

According to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Brown has a 51 percent chance to defeat Husted and is anticipated to be one of the tightest races in this year’s midterms.

Following Obama’s Cleveland rally, he will travel north to Detroit to campaign with Michigan’s Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is facing former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

DDHQ has El-Sayed holding a steady lead over Rogers, 68 percent to 32 percent, respectively.

Former Vice President Harris will also be hitting the campaign trail on Saturday, meeting up with Democratic Senate candidate Chris Pappas (N.H.) in Portsmouth, N.H.

Pappas is facing off against Republican challenger John Sununu for the chance to succeed Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.).

Despite the Democrat frenzy, Trump is not done with his midterm tour. The president will hold a 7 p.m. rally in Perry Ga. in an attempt to boost Republican Senate candidate Rep. Mike Collins, who is going up against incumbent Democrat Sen. Jon Ossoff.

The president will also rally in Port Huron, Mich., Corinth, Miss. and Lubbock and Waco, Texas next week.

Follow live below.

data.title: Jennings: Ramaswamy's campaign tactics 'worst politics you could imagine'
data.description:
Republican commentator Scott Jennings took a swipe at Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R) for using a controversial campaign ad featuring his opponent’s estranged mother.

The ad, which Ramaswamy’s campaign is now spending $4 million to broadcast statewide, features Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, accusing Acton of being a “liar” her whole life.

Acton was removed from her mother’s custody at age 12 after her stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her. Arthur remained with Acton’s stepfather until his death.

According to legal filings Acton’s campaign shared with The Hill, Arthur was previously convicted with theft and animal cruelty, though one of her sentences was vacated.

Jennings, a Trump ally who frequently defends the president and the GOP on CNN, joins a growing list of Republicans pushing back against the ad.

The conservative political commentator told CNN’s Anderson Cooper Friday that the ad is “not good” morally and is a political misstep.

“What you’re talking about here is Amy Acton’s mother is basically saying, ‘I don’t trust 12-year-old Amy Acton, who was quite possibly raped in my own home, to be governor,’” Jennings said. “It’s a ludicrous sort of argument that they’re making.”

“This is probably the worst politics you could imagine, and it’s bringing a lot of attention to Amy Acton’s story, her narrative,” he added.

Ramaswamy has doubled down on the ad, accusing Acton of “lying about an ad that is about lying.” President Trump and Vice President Vance have repeatedly defended the Ohio Republican, with Vance saying he was “disgusted” by those in his party who criticized use of the ad.

Trump continues to say that he trusts Acton’s mother, and told reporters at the White House Friday that he did not “know anything about a stepfather,” telling the reporter who asked the question to be “quiet.”

“Vivek should keep it up,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday.

Jennings said the White House “absolutely” could brief the president on Acton’s side of the story.

”I don’t know what he knows or what he doesn’t know,” Jennings said. “They absolutely could [brief him], and if they did, he would learn the terrible details of this.”

Polling suggests Acton’s lead in the gubernatorial race was already growing ahead of the scandal, and nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ gives Acton a 62 percent chance of beating Ramaswamy.

Jennings said the ad could have backfired because it does not help the former presidential candidate’s likability, which the CNN commentator said is one of his biggest challenges in this election.

“One of Ramaswamy’s key candidate deficiencies is likability. Not certain this is doing anything to help that,” Jennings said. “It was a problem for him in the ‘24 presidential primary, and it’s a problem for him in this governor’s race.”

data.title: Ukraine reports Starlink operating again after slowdown
data.description:
Ukraine’s Starlink satellite links have been restored after the country experienced limitations with accessing this critical technology, the Ukrainian defense minister said Saturday. 

SpaceX’s military-grade version of Starlink, called Starshield, supports Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. 

Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told reporters on a call that the ministry’s monitoring systems now reported stable connections for objects traveling faster than around 250 miles per hour. 

“The Ministry of Defence’s monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield,” Khmara told reporters, according to Reuters. “We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable.”

Khmara attributed the change to “direct dialogue” between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Trump administration. He added that the outcome mattered most “for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.” 

This announcement follows tensions between Kyiv and the U.S. over President Trump’s Russian diesel deal and decision to postpone sanctions on Moscow — two decisions Zelensky warned endangered Ukrainians in their ongoing war against Russia. 

Zelensky said in Friday remarks that Ukraine’s military was still struggling with Starlink satellite speeds limited at around 100 mph. 

“The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there, and the speed has not been restored,” the Ukrainian president said. 

Earlier that day, Trump told reporters on the White House South Lawn that he had not spoken with SpaceX leader Elon Musk about the restricted Starlink speeds in Ukraine but said he “might have to” if the issue was not fixed. 

This week, Russia accepted an invitation to resume three-way negotiations with Ukraine and the U.S.

Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed “in principle” to restart talks after Nov. 10, according to his foreign affairs adviser. 

Additionally, the White House said Friday that first lady Melania Trump helped secure a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that will begin Thursday in the front-line city of Oleshky. 

This action will “allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway,” according to the White House.

data.title: Critics should do their homework before attacking Arabic language programs
data.description:
I expected criticism when I agreed to consult with the Embassy of Qatar on its education initiatives. But I did not foresee the torrent of falsehoods that would come.

Qatar plays an important and sometimes complicated role in the Middle East. I thought my experience as a former secretary of Education could help clarify at least that part of its activities. I did not expect a Qatari program that helps American students learn Arabic to be portrayed as an effort to “infiltrate” our public schools.

That is the argument being advanced by organizations that have raised concerns about Qatar Foundation International, which provided grants to support Arabic language programs in American schools. The fact is, America needs more language education, not less. And scrutiny needs to yield to the facts.

Under the Qatar Foundation International program, American schools retained control of what was taught. The funding was transparent. Students got a legitimate educational opportunity to learn a new language. They got only that and nothing more. 

Critics cite an instance from P.S. 261 in Brooklyn where a classroom map labeled the area of Israel as Palestine. Qatar Foundation International had supported an Arab language program at the school, and the map quickly became part of a larger narrative about Qatari influence.

But there is an important difference between funding a program and supplying a particular classroom item. New York City Schools Chancellor David Banks testified before Congress that the teacher, a New York City employee, had obtained the map with her own funds while visiting Jerusalem. The map had nothing to do with Qatar Foundation International.

The same is true in New Haven, Connecticut, where Qatar Foundation International has supported Arabic instruction since 2018. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies includes New Haven in its exposé-style presentation that frames foreign-language education grants as a national security and foreign influence threat.

But Mayor Justin Elicker and Superintendent Madeline Negrón looked into the claims. Elicker said publicly that he had examined the program extensively and found that it was “purely teaching students Arabic.”

In June, Qatar Foundation International announced that it was ending operations in the U.S. after 17 years of supporting Arabic language education. Schools and teachers that relied on its grants will have to look elsewhere to sustain those programs. Some critics, including an official from the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism and Policy, celebrated the news.

That reaction is deeply misguided. American students need more opportunities to study strategically important languages. The disappearance of funding for Arabic instruction is nothing to celebrate.

The bipartisan Commission on Language Learning of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences concluded that language skills matter to America’s economic competitiveness, national security and ability to engage with the world. It recommended that every child should have the opportunity to learn a language other than English. It also suggested that partnerships involving schools, governments, philanthropies, businesses and communities make that possible.

Arabic is one of the world’s most widely spoken languages and is important to U.S. diplomacy, national security and business.

Germany’s government supports German language programs in hundreds of American schools. Spain’s Ministry of Education places Spanish language assistants in schools across the U.S. Italy offers grants that help cover the salaries of Italian language teachers. Japan supports Japanese language instruction and sends teaching assistants to American schools.

We do not describe these programs as attempts to infiltrate American classrooms. We recognize them for what they are: countries promoting their languages and schools taking advantage of resources that expand opportunities for students.

Arabic should be treated no differently. In fact, Qatar Foundation International’s grants were indeed no different. They provided resources to teach an important language to American students. And that’s all.

Outside funding of Arabic language studies should be transparent, of course. School districts should control the curriculum. Parents should know what is being taught. Political or religious indoctrination has no place in a public-school language class.

I come to this debate with some personal experience.

I recently resigned from the Middle East Media Research Institute. I once strongly supported its mission of bringing greater transparency to Middle Eastern discourse by translating and publishing primary-source material. But in my view, the organization has moved too far from that mission and toward ideological advocacy, including in its treatment of Qatar and the promotion of conspiratorial reports about the nation.

Arabic should not be treated differently from German, Spanish, Italian or Japanese because of contemporary politics. America will not become stronger by giving its children fewer opportunities to understand the world. We need transparency and, of course, we need local control.

But most importantly, we need more language education, not less.

William J. Bennett is a former secretary of Education.

data.title: Early voting surges in battleground states as Democrats outpace GOP gains
data.description:
Early voting is surging in several key battleground states, giving Democrats hope that their strength in midterm polling could translate into a turnout advantage in November.

In North Carolina, more than 1.2 million early ballots have been accepted, a 37 percent increase from the same point leading up to the 2022 midterms, according to an analysis released Friday by Catawba College political scientist Michael Bitzer. 

That growth — which includes both in-person and mail-in ballots — has been driven by a 47 percent increase among registered Democrats and a 60 percent increase in participation among unaffiliated voters. Early voting among Republicans is up 2.6 percent.

Similar patterns are emerging elsewhere, with high turnout especially pronounced in historically Republican-leaning states with competitive Senate races this cycle.

More than 23 million ballots have been accepted nationwide, compared with more than 15 million reported at a similar point ahead of the 2022 midterms. In Kansas, early voting is up roughly 69 percent, while it’s up 41 percent in Maine and 24 percent in Iowa, according to a New York Times analysis of state election records and voter data through Thursday.

Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political science professor who tracks early voting, said Democrats and unaffiliated voters are similarly outpacing Republicans in turnout gains compared to 2022 across states where he has comparable party registration data — including Kansas, Maine, Iowa and Nebraska.

“It’s the same pattern. Democrats and unaffiliateds are engaged. Republicans are not as engaged,” McDonald told The Hill, adding, “And it explains why you might be seeing this shift of the battleground into these red states. Overall, there’s just more engagement among Democrats.”

McDonald cautioned that there is a range of factors that can affect states’ early voting numbers, including changing timelines for when mail-in ballots are sent out. 

There are also limits to what early voting data can reveal. Not all states record party registration, and there’s no guarantee that a voter’s party affiliation will match that of the candidate they choose to support.

But McDonald said the early voting patterns give credence to polls showing Democrats in a strong position heading into Election Day.

“The early voting data is just telling me that what we know from the polling data is correct. That yes, the polling is not telling us something wrong. There’s not some big polling miss on the horizon,” McDonald said.

In Texas, Democrats are hoping Senate nominee James Talarico can end the party’s more than three-decade drought in statewide elections. But Texas does not register voters by party, making it harder to determine whether Democrats’ strength in polling is translating into an early turnout advantage. 

Decision Desk HQ’s modeling suggests a narrower partisan gap than in some other states. Of the 2.06 million ballots cast in person or returned by mail as of Thursday, an estimated 44.3 percent came from Democratic voters and 43.7 percent came from Republicans. Among Hispanic early voters, the model estimates Democrats outnumber Republicans by roughly 2.5 to 1. 

Democrats are also pointing to strong participation in Travis County, a Democratic stronghold that includes Austin. 

More than 158,000 in-person ballots were cast during the first four days of early voting, up roughly 61 percent from the same point in 2022 and 19 percent from 2018, according to a compilation of state election data provided by the county Democratic Party. The county’s registered electorate has also grown since 2018, so the increase in ballots does not necessarily represent a higher participation rate. 

“In Travis County, where Democrats really need to run up the score, we’re beating 2022 and 2018 turnout levels—elections when Beto [O’Rourke] was on the ballot—and pacing towards 2024 turnout,” Luke Warford, chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said in a statement to The Hill.

But higher turnout in Democratic strongholds alone will not be enough for Talarico to win in November, said Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston. 

“Democrats don’t just need high turnout to win statewide. They need urban margins large enough to overcome rural margins, and Republicans’ rural floor has risen since 2018,” Rottinghaus said. “High turnout is necessary for Democrats, but not sufficient.”

He also noted that high turnout this cycle is “not only a Democratic story,” saying there’s a “slight purple tinge to the turnout so far,” and redder, rural areas are “slow out of the gate but catching up.”

In Georgia, where Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is favored to fend off his Republican challenger, voters also do not register by party, “so we can only make guesses about who is turning out to vote based on geography and demographic factors,” said Andra Gillespie, a political scientist at Emory University.

Early voting is slightly higher this year, with approximately 1.5 million ballots cast through Thursday, up from roughly 1.4 million at the same point in 2022, according to the Times analysis. 

Gillespie said Democrats likely benefit from elevated turnout among Black voters and among voters living in the metropolitan areas of Atlanta, Athens, Savannah, Macon and Augusta. But she said participation is also strong in traditionally Republican areas, like Cherokee and Forsyth counties.

“Democrats have been trying to make inroads there, so it is not clear whether the people turning out are Democrats or Republicans yet,” she said. 

In Virginia, where Democrats are targeting several GOP-held House seats, nearly 930,000 early ballots had been cast through Thursday, roughly 80 percent more than at the same point in 2022, according to the Virginia Public Access Project.

“Early voting in Virginia has been concentrated in congressional districts where Republicans are playing defense, not offense,” University of Mary Washington political scientist Stephen Farnsworth said. 

He noted that, although Virginians do not register by party, “polling shows far more interest in voting among Democrats than Republicans.”

Several factors could still influence turnout in the next week. Republicans have time to narrow the participation gap, and GOP voters have historically turned out more heavily on Election Day. 

President Trump’s shifting message on mail-in ballots could also affect voter behavior. He has repeatedly attacked and tried to restrict mail voting but has more recently encouraged Republicans to vote early or by mail.

“The big question this year is whether Republicans are more likely to take advantage of early voting now that President Trump has relaxed his rhetoric about why one should only vote on Election Day,” Gillespie said. “If Republicans vote alongside Democrats in early voting, then we may not see Election Day surges in voting in Republican areas that we have seen in the past.”

McDonald, meanwhile, said concerns about mail voting could push some Democrats to vote in person, reducing the likelihood of their ballots being rejected. More than half a million mail ballots were rejected for various reasons in 2024, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. 

“If there are fewer people who are voting by mail, and it’s particularly Democrats, that means that there are going to be fewer Democratic rejected mail ballots,” McDonald said.

“Trump may have inadvertently done a favor to the Democrats by encouraging their voters to vote in person, and we’re seeing that in the in-person early voting.”
